problems.title: Product of Array Except Self
problems.description:
Given an integer array `nums`, return an array `answer` where `answer[i]` is the product of every element of `nums` except `nums[i]`.

Do not use division, and aim for O(n) time. The product of any prefix or suffix of `nums` fits in a 32-bit integer.

examples.explanation: The single zero wipes out every product that includes it.

problems.complexity: O(n) time, O(1) extra space (excluding output)
hints: Answer[i] is (product of everything left of i) times (product of everything right of i).
Compute the left products in one pass and store them in the output array.
Walk right to left keeping a running suffix product, multiplying it into the output array in place.

solutions.python:
def product_except_self(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    out = [1] * n
    left = 1
    for i in range(n):
        out[i] = left
        left *= nums[i]
    right = 1
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        out[i] *= right
        right *= nums[i]
    return out

problems.title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
problems.description:
Given an unsorted integer array `nums`, return the length of the longest run of consecutive integers that can be formed from its values (for example `4, 5, 6, 7`). The numbers do not need to be adjacent in the array.

Your algorithm must run in O(n) time.
hints: Sorting gives O(n log n). How can a hash set let you skip the sort?
A run only needs to be counted from its smallest element: x is a start if x - 1 is not in the set.
Put all values in a set. For each start value, walk x, x+1, x+2... while present and track the best length.

problems.title: 3Sum
problems.description:
Given an integer array `nums`, return all unique triplets `[a, b, c]` such that `a + b + c == 0`. Each triplet uses three different indices, and the result must not contain duplicate triplets (the same three values in any order count as the same triplet).

You may return the triplets and the values inside each triplet in any order.
problems.complexity: O(n^2) time, O(1) extra space (excluding output)
hints: Fixing one number turns the problem into a two-sum on the rest.
Sort first. Then for each index i, use two pointers on the sorted suffix to look for pairs summing to -nums[i].
Skip repeated values for i and, after finding a triplet, for the left and right pointers so duplicates never appear.

problems.title: Trapping Rain Water
problems.description:
You are given an array `height` of non-negative integers describing an elevation map where each bar has width 1. After rain, water collects in the gaps between bars.

Return the total units of water that stay trapped.
hints: Water above bar i is limited by min(tallest bar to its left, tallest bar to its right) minus height[i].
Precomputing left-max and right-max arrays works in O(n) space. Can two pointers avoid the arrays?
Keep pointers l and r with running maxima. Always advance the side with the smaller max; its water level is determined by that max.

solutions.python:
def trap(height):
    l, r = 0, len(height) - 1
    lm = rm = 0
    total = 0
    while l < r:
        if height[l] < height[r]:
            lm = max(lm, height[l])
            total += lm - height[l]
            l += 1
        else:
            rm = max(rm, height[r])
            total += rm - height[r]
            r -= 1
    return total

problems.title: Minimum Window Substring
problems.description:
Given two strings `s` and `t`, return the shortest substring of `s` that contains every character of `t`, counting duplicates (if `t` has two `A`s the window needs at least two `A`s).

If no such substring exists return the empty string. If several windows tie for the shortest length, return the leftmost one.
constraints: s and t consist of English letters
problems.complexity: O(|s| + |t|) time, O(1) space for a fixed alphabet
hints: Check every substring is O(n^3). Think of a window [l, r] that grows and shrinks.
Count the characters needed from t. Expand r until the window satisfies all counts, then shrink l while it still does.
Track how many distinct required characters are currently satisfied so each window check is O(1); record the best window whenever it is valid.

problems.title: Sliding Window Maximum
problems.description:
You are given an integer array `nums` and a window size `k`. The window starts at the left end of the array and moves one position to the right at a time until it reaches the end.

Return an array containing the maximum value inside the window at each position.
hints: Scanning each window costs O(n*k). Which elements can never be a future maximum?
If a newer element is larger than an older one in the window, the older one is useless. A monotonic deque captures this.
Keep indices in a deque with decreasing values: pop from the back while the new value is bigger, pop from the front when its index leaves the window; the front is the max.

problems.title: Longest Repeating Character Replacement
problems.description:
Given a string `s` of uppercase letters and an integer `k`, you may change at most `k` characters of `s` to any other uppercase letter.

Return the length of the longest substring that can be made to consist of a single repeated letter using at most `k` changes.

examples.explanation: Change the B at index 3: AAAA.

constraints: s consists of uppercase English letters
hints: For a fixed window, how many replacements are needed to make it uniform?
That count is window length minus the frequency of its most common letter. The window is valid if it is at most k.
Slide a window with a frequency table; grow right each step and move left only when (length - maxFreq) > k. maxFreq never needs to decrease.

problems.title: Permutation in String
problems.description:
Given two strings `s1` and `s2`, return `true` if `s2` contains a substring that is a rearrangement (permutation) of `s1`, and `false` otherwise.

The substring must be contiguous in `s2` and use exactly the letters of `s1`.
constraints: Both strings consist of lowercase English letters
hints: Two strings are permutations of each other exactly when their letter counts match.
Only windows of length len(s1) in s2 matter, so slide one fixed-size window.
Keep a 26-slot count difference; add the incoming letter, remove the outgoing letter, and track how many slots are nonzero (or compare arrays) after each move.

problems.title: Daily Temperatures
problems.description: Given an array `temperatures` of daily readings, return an array `answer` where `answer[i]` is the number of days you must wait after day `i` to see a strictly warmer temperature. If no warmer day exists, `answer[i]` is `0`.
hints: Brute force looks ahead from each day, O(n^2). What work is repeated?
Days still waiting for a warmer day form a stack whose temperatures are non-increasing from bottom to top.
Scan left to right; while the current temperature exceeds the temperature at the stack top, pop that index and set its answer to the index difference. Then push the current index.

problems.title: Largest Rectangle in Histogram
problems.description:
You are given an array `heights` representing a histogram whose bars each have width 1. Return the area of the largest rectangle that fits entirely inside the histogram.

The rectangle's sides must align with the bars: it spans a contiguous range of bars and its height is limited by the shortest bar in that range.

examples.explanation: Bars of height 5 and 6 give 5 x 2 = 10.

hints: For each bar, the best rectangle using it as the shortest bar extends left and right until a shorter bar is found.
Finding the nearest shorter bar on each side is a 'next smaller element' problem that a monotonic stack solves.

Keep a stack of bars with increasing heights. When a shorter bar arrives, pop taller bars and compute their area using the new top of the stack as the left boundary. Append a 0 sentinel to flush at the end.

solutions.python:
def largest_rectangle_area(heights):
    st = []
    best = 0
    hs = heights + [0]
    for i, h in enumerate(hs):
        start = i
        while st and st[-1][1] >= h:
            idx, ph = st.pop()
            best = max(best, ph * (i - idx))
            start = idx
        st.append((start, h))
    return best

problems.title: Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation
problems.description:
You are given an array of strings `tokens` forming a valid arithmetic expression in Reverse Polish Notation (postfix). Valid operators are `+`, `-`, `*` and `/`; every other token is an integer.

Evaluate the expression and return the result as an integer. Division between two integers truncates toward zero. The expression is always valid, never divides by zero, and every intermediate value fits in a 32-bit signed integer.
constraints: Tokens are integers in [-200, 200] or one of + - * /
hints: In postfix form an operator always applies to the two most recent results.
A stack holds the operands seen so far.
Push numbers; on an operator pop b then a, compute a op b, and push the result. Truncate division toward zero (watch negative numbers).

problems.title: Car Fleet
problems.description:
Several cars drive in the same direction along a single-lane road toward a destination `target` miles away. Car `i` starts at `position[i]` and travels at a constant `speed[i]`, all positions being distinct.

A car can never pass another. If a faster car catches up to a slower one ahead of it, it must slow down and drive bumper to bumper, forming a fleet that moves at the slower car's speed. A single car also counts as a fleet, and cars that meet exactly at the destination belong to the same fleet.

Return the number of distinct fleets that arrive at the destination.

examples.explanation: Cars at 10 and 8 merge, cars at 5 and 3 merge, the car at 0 is alone.

problems.complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
hints: Only the time each car would need to reach the target on its own matters.
Process cars from the closest to the target backwards. A car whose arrival time is not greater than the fleet ahead of it merges into that fleet.
Sort by position descending, compute time = (target - pos) / speed, and count how many times a car's time is strictly greater than the max time so far.

problems.title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
problems.description:
An array of distinct integers was sorted in ascending order and then rotated at an unknown pivot, so for example `[0,1,2,4,5,6,7]` might become `[4,5,6,7,0,1,2]`.

Given the rotated array `nums` and an integer `target`, return the index of `target`, or `-1` if it is not present. Your solution must run in O(log n) time.
hints: At least one half of the array around the midpoint is always sorted.
Decide which half is sorted by comparing nums[lo] with nums[mid].
If target lies inside the sorted half's value range, search that half; otherwise search the other half. Repeat until found or the range is empty.

problems.title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
problems.description:
A sorted array of distinct integers has been rotated an unknown number of times (possibly zero). Given the rotated array `nums`, return its smallest element.

Your algorithm must run in O(log n) time.
hints: The minimum is the 'break point' where the order drops.
Compare nums[mid] to nums[hi]: if mid is larger, the minimum is to the right of mid.
Binary search with lo < hi: if nums[mid] > nums[hi] then lo = mid + 1, else hi = mid. When lo == hi, that's the minimum.

problems.title: Koko Eating Bananas
problems.description:
Koko has `n` piles of bananas, where pile `i` holds `piles[i]` bananas. She must finish all of them within `h` hours.

Each hour she picks one pile and eats up to `k` bananas from it. If the pile has fewer than `k` bananas she finishes it and does nothing else that hour. Return the minimum integer eating speed `k` that lets her finish within `h` hours.

examples.explanation: Every pile needs its own hour.

problems.complexity: O(n log m) time where m = max(piles), O(1) space
hints: The answer lies between 1 and the largest pile.
If speed k works, every larger speed works too. That monotonic property allows binary search on the answer.
For a candidate k the hours needed are the sum of ceil(pile / k). Search for the smallest k whose total is at most h.

problems.title: Median of Two Sorted Arrays
problems.description:
Given two sorted arrays `nums1` and `nums2`, return the median of the combined sorted sequence as a number.

If the total count is odd the median is the middle element; if even, it is the average of the two middle elements (which may be a decimal such as `2.5`). The overall run time must be O(log(m + n)).
constraints: 0 <= nums1.length, nums2.length <= 1000 (at least one is non-empty)
hints: Merging both arrays works in O(m + n) but ignores the O(log) requirement.
The median splits the combined elements into equal left and right halves. Choose how many elements the left half takes from the shorter array; the rest come from the other.

Binary search the cut i in the shorter array (cut j = half - i in the other). A cut is correct when maxLeft of each array <= minRight of the other; use -inf/+inf at the edges, then derive the median from the four boundary values.

problems.title: Reverse Linked List
problems.description:
A singly linked list is given as an array `head` holding the node values from head to tail (an empty array is an empty list). Reverse the list and return the values of the reversed list in an array.

In an interview you would rewire the `next` pointers in place; here, implement the same pointer-reversal idea by building a linked list from the array internally, reversing it, and converting it back, or reason with the array form directly.
problems.complexity: O(n) time, O(1) extra space for the pointer version
hints: Each node's next pointer must end up pointing at the node before it.
Walk the list with three references: previous, current, and the saved next node.
For each node: save current.next, point current.next at previous, then advance previous and current. Return previous when current is null.

problems.title: Merge k Sorted Lists
problems.description:
You are given `lists`, an array of `k` sorted linked lists, each encoded as an array of its node values in ascending order (an empty array is an empty list).

Merge all lists into one sorted list and return its values as an array. Think of it as merging linked lists: repeatedly take the smallest head among the k lists.
constraints: The total number of nodes is at most 10^5
problems.complexity: O(N log k) time, O(k) space (N = total nodes)
hints: Merging two sorted lists is easy. How might you reuse that for k lists?
Either merge lists pairwise in rounds (divide and conquer), or always pull the smallest current head using a min-heap of size k.
Push (value, list index, position) for each non-empty list into a min-heap. Pop the smallest, append it to the output, and push the next element from the same list.

solutions.python:
import heapq


def merge_k_lists(lists):
    heap = [(lst[0], i, 0) for i, lst in enumerate(lists) if lst]
    heapq.heapify(heap)
    out = []
    while heap:
        v, i, j = heapq.heappop(heap)
        out.append(v)
        if j + 1 < len(lists[i]):
            heapq.heappush(heap, (lists[i][j + 1], i, j + 1))
    return out

problems.title: LRU Cache
problems.description:
Design a Least Recently Used (LRU) cache with a fixed `capacity`. It supports two operations, both in O(1) average time:

- `get(key)` returns the value stored for `key`, or `-1` if it is absent. A successful get makes the key the most recently used.
- `put(key, value)` inserts or updates the key and makes it the most recently used. If the insertion pushes the size above `capacity`, evict the least recently used key.

In this exercise you implement a function `lru_cache(capacity, operations)` that creates the cache, then runs each operation in order. Each operation is `["put", key, value]` or `["get", key]`. Return a list with one entry per operation: `null` for every put, and the result for every get.

examples.explanation: Putting 3 evicts key 2, the least recently used.

hints: You need fast lookup by key and fast reordering by recency.
A hash map gives O(1) lookup; a doubly linked list (or an ordered map) tracks recency order in O(1) moves.

On get/put, move the key to the most-recent end. On overflow, remove the key at the least-recent end. An ordered dict / JS Map does this directly; otherwise combine a hash map with a doubly linked list.

problems.title: Insert Interval
problems.description:
You are given a list of non-overlapping intervals `intervals`, each `[start, end]`, sorted by start, and a new interval `newInterval`.

Insert `newInterval` so the list stays sorted by start and has no overlaps, merging any intervals that overlap it (touching endpoints such as `[1,3]` and `[3,5]` count as overlapping). Return the resulting list.

examples.explanation: The new interval swallows three intervals.

constraints: intervals is sorted by start and non-overlapping
hints: The intervals fall into three groups: entirely before, overlapping, and entirely after the new one.
Copy intervals that end before newInterval starts. Then merge every interval whose start is <= newInterval's end.
While merging, set start = min(starts) and end = max(ends). Append the merged interval, then copy the remaining intervals.

solutions.python:
def insert_interval(intervals, new_interval):
    res = []
    s, e = new_interval
    i, n = 0, len(intervals)
    while i < n and intervals[i][1] < s:
        res.append(intervals[i])
        i += 1
    while i < n and intervals[i][0] <= e:
        s = min(s, intervals[i][0])
        e = max(e, intervals[i][1])
        i += 1
    res.append([s, e])
    res.extend(intervals[i:])
    return res

problems.title: Spiral Matrix
problems.description: Given an `m x n` matrix, return all of its elements in spiral order: start at the top-left corner, move right along the top row, then down the right column, then left along the bottom row, then up the left column, and keep spiralling inward until every element has been visited once.
problems.complexity: O(m * n) time, O(1) extra space (excluding output)
hints: The spiral is a sequence of shrinking rectangular layers.
Track four boundaries: top, bottom, left, right. Walk each side in turn, then move the boundary inward.
After walking the top row and right column, check top <= bottom and left <= right before walking the bottom row and left column, so single rows or columns are not visited twice.

problems.title: Rotate Image
problems.description:
You are given an `n x n` matrix representing an image. Rotate it 90 degrees clockwise and return the rotated matrix.

In an interview you would be asked to do this in place without allocating another matrix; do the same here (modify the input and return it), using O(1) extra space.
hints: Where does the element at row r, column c end up after a clockwise rotation?
A clockwise rotation equals a transpose followed by reversing each row.
Swap matrix[i][j] with matrix[j][i] for j > i (transpose in place), then reverse every row in place.
